title: Questions to Ask Before You Rent a Flat in India (And Exactly How to Ask Them)
seoTitle: Questions to Ask Before Renting a Flat in India
description: The exact questions to ask an owner, a watchman and a neighbour before renting a flat in India, and what a vague or evasive answer really tells you.
excerpt: Not a vague list of things to consider — the actual sentences to say, who to say them to, and how to read the answer you get back.

author.name: The StayOnMap team
author.role: Renters who learned these questions the expensive way

faq.q: What is the single most useful question to ask a landlord?
faq.a: "What did the last tenant complain about?" It assumes a problem existed rather than asking whether one did, so it is much harder to answer with a flat no. An honest owner names something small and often tells you how they fixed it. An owner who insists there has never been a single complaint is managing you rather than informing you.

faq.q: Is it rude to ask why the previous tenant left?
faq.a: No, and most owners answer it without a second thought — job change, marriage, bought their own place. It only becomes awkward when the real reason is something about the flat, which is precisely why the question is worth asking. Ask it casually, as though the answer is obviously going to be ordinary.

faq.q: What should I ask the watchman or security guard?
faq.a: Water timings and how they change in summer, how often the power goes and whether the generator covers the flats, noise at night, safety after dark, and parking. Then the two that matter most: whether the last tenant left on good terms, and whether people usually get their deposit back from this owner. He has no stake in you taking the flat, which is what makes his answers valuable.

faq.q: How do I ask about the deposit refund without sounding suspicious?
faq.a: Ask it as a process question rather than a trust question: "How and when does the deposit come back, and what would typically be deducted?" That is a reasonable thing for anyone handing over several lakh rupees to want to know. Then ask specifically whether repainting is charged to the tenant, because that is the most commonly disputed deduction.

faq.q: Should I get the answers in writing?
faq.a: The ones that cost money, yes. Deposit refund timeline, what gets deducted, who pays for repairs, notice period in both directions, and any renewal escalation belong in the agreement, not in a WhatsApp thread. If an owner is happy to say something out loud but reluctant to write it down, treat that reluctance as information.

faq.q: What if the owner gets annoyed by my questions?
faq.a: That is useful data, not a failed viewing. You have just seen how this person responds when you need something from them, which is exactly what will happen in month seven when the water motor fails. Most owners actually prefer a tenant who asks about the notice period, because it suggests someone who plans to honour it.

body:
Meera almost took the flat. Second floor, decent light, rent slightly under what she'd budgeted, and the owner was pleasant in that unhurried way that makes you relax. She was doing the final walk-through when she asked him something she'd only thought of on the stairs: "How long has this been empty?"

He paused. Then said, "Four months, maybe five."

That's the whole story. A well-priced two-bedroom in a decent Chennai neighbourhood sitting empty for five months isn't a mystery, it's a message. She asked a follow-up and got something vague about people being fussy. So she went down and asked the watchman instead. Water came for forty minutes in the morning, he said, and the second-floor line was the worst in the building. Two tenants had left over it.

Meera didn't take the flat. Total cost of that decision: one question, asked out loud, on the stairs.

Most renters never ask it. They ask about rent, about the deposit, about when they can move in, and then they sign. Not because they're careless — because asking feels rude, and nobody ever taught them which questions actually pull information loose.

This article is the wording. Not a vague list of "things to consider" but the actual sentences, who to say them to, why each one works, and what it means when the answer is mushy.

## Why we don't ask, and why that's expensive

Three things stop people.

**You feel like a supplicant.** In a tight market with more renters than flats, you're aware that the owner has options and you don't. Asking hard questions feels like a way to lose the flat. So you stay agreeable, sign, and discover the water schedule in week two.

**You don't know what's askable.** Nobody tells you it's normal to ask why the last tenant left. It feels nosy. It isn't — it's the single most informative question in the whole conversation, and any reasonable owner answers it without blinking.

**You're being managed.** A viewing is a sales situation, even a soft one. The owner picks the hour. Morning viewings hide evening noise; a Sunday viewing hides the weekday parking crush.

Here's the reframe that helps: **you are not asking for a favour, you are about to hand a near-stranger several lakh rupees.** Ask the questions you'd ask before any other transaction that size.

## Questions for the owner about money

Money questions are the easiest to ask because everyone expects them, and the easiest to get wrong because people only ask about rent.

The one that matters most, and almost nobody phrases properly:

> "What's the total amount I'll be transferring to you before I get the keys — rent, deposit, maintenance, anything else? Can you give me the full figure?"

Ask for **one number**. Not the components — the total. This is the question that surfaces the advance maintenance, the society move-in charge, the "token" that turns out to be non-refundable, the one-time water connection fee. If the number that comes back is different from the one you'd worked out in your head, you've just learned something before it cost you anything. Our piece on the [hidden costs of renting in India](/blog/hidden-costs-of-renting-in-india) covers the specific line items that tend to appear here.

Then, in order:

**"What does the maintenance charge actually cover?"** You want to hear specifics: lift, common-area power, security salaries, water tanker, corpus fund. If the answer is a shrug and "it's what the association decides," ask whether you or the owner pays it, and whether it can change mid-year.

**"Which bills come to me separately?"** Electricity is usually yours. Water may or may not be. Piped gas, internet, generator diesel, garbage collection — ask about each one out loud rather than assuming. And specifically: is there a charge when a water tanker is called? Between February and June that's a monthly reality in a lot of buildings, split among the flats.

**"How and when does the deposit come back? What would you deduct for?"** This is the question that predicts the last week of your tenancy. You want a specific mechanism — "bank transfer within fifteen days of handover, after adjusting any unpaid bills." What you don't want is "we'll settle it, don't worry." Ask the follow-up plainly: "Would repainting be deducted from my deposit, or is that your cost?" Repainting is one of the most common deductions and one of the most commonly disputed, so get the answer before you move in rather than after. Our [guide to security deposits in India](/blog/security-deposits-in-india) explains what tends to be defensible and what doesn't.

**"If I take the flat, when do you want the money, and what receipt will I get?"** Any reluctance to give a written receipt for a lakh-plus transfer is a serious signal, not a small one.

## Questions for the owner about the home itself

These are the ones that need to be asked *conversationally*, because they're the ones people get defensive about.

**"How old is the building?"** Simple, and it reframes everything else. A twenty-eight-year-old building isn't bad — but plumbing, wiring and waterproofing all have lifespans, and you should know where you are on that clock.

**"When was the bathroom last worked on? Any leak or seepage issues in this stack?"** Say "stack" if you can — it tells the owner you know that bathroom problems travel vertically through a building, and you'll get a straighter answer. A flat can be spotless and still sit below a leaking pipe.

**"Where does the water come from — borewell, corporation, or both? What hours does it run?"** Ask for hours, not adjectives. "Water is not a problem here" is not an answer. "Corporation supply, roughly 6 to 8 in the morning, and we run a tanker maybe twice a month in summer" is an answer. Then ask: "And in April and May?"

**"Is there a generator? Does it cover this flat, or just the lift and common areas?"** Rarely asked, and it matters — plenty of buildings have backup for the lift and the corridor lights and nothing at all inside the flats.

**"What did the last tenant complain about?"** The best question in the article, and it works because of how it's framed. You're not asking "is anything wrong" — which invites a no. You're assuming something existed, because something always does, and you're inviting the owner to tell you which thing. An honest owner will say "the geyser was slow, I replaced it" or "they didn't like the road noise." A defensive one will insist there were no complaints ever, which tells you they'd rather manage you than inform you.

**"Why did they leave?"** Job change, marriage, bought their own place, moved cities — all fine and all easily verifiable in tone. "They had some issues" without elaboration is worth pushing on once, gently: "Issues with the flat, or something else?"

**"How long has it been vacant?"** Meera's question. A well-priced flat in a good location that's been empty for months has a reason, and the reason is rarely visible during a twenty-minute viewing.

**"Who handles repairs — you, a caretaker, or do I arrange it and adjust against rent?"** Get the process, and a name and number if there's a caretaker. This is the difference between a leaking tap fixed in two days and one you eventually fix yourself.

**"Has anything water-logged here in the last few monsoons — the flat, the parking, or the road outside?"** Ask about the road specifically. A dry flat on an unusable street is still a problem for four months a year.

## Questions for the owner about the terms

These belong in the conversation *before* the agreement is drafted, not after it's printed.

**"Is there a lock-in period, and what happens if I have to leave inside it?"** Lock-in is common and not unreasonable in itself. What matters is the consequence — some agreements forfeit the deposit entirely, others require you to pay rent for the balance of the lock-in.

**"What's the notice period, both ways?"** Both ways. Some agreements ask three months from the tenant and give one from the owner. Ask for symmetry; if you don't get it, at least know.

**"If we renew after eleven months, how much would the rent go up?"** Nail this down early. An unspecified escalation is a negotiation you'll have from a much weaker position a year from now, once you're settled and moving would cost you.

**"Any restrictions I should know about — guests staying over, pets, food, working from home?"** Ask all four together and let the owner pick which one he has an opinion about. Some societies restrict what looks like commercial use; some impose food restrictions, whatever anyone's view of that. And if pets matter to you, get it into the agreement — a verbal yes from an owner does not bind a society.

**"Who pays for what if something breaks — the geyser, the motor, the taps?"** The general convention is that the owner handles structural and fixed equipment while the tenant handles consumables and their own damage, but conventions aren't rules. Once you've agreed, get it written down; our [guide to rental agreements](/blog/rental-agreements-in-india) covers which clauses are worth arguing over.

## The people with no reason to sell you the flat

This is the part most renters skip, and it's the highest-value ten minutes of the entire search. The owner wants the flat let. The broker, if there is one, wants the commission. The **watchman and the neighbours want nothing from you at all** — the only genuinely disinterested sources you have.

Go back at a different hour — early evening on a weekday is ideal. Be friendly, be brief, and open with something that signals you're not an inspector:

> "Hi, I'm thinking of taking the flat on the second floor. Just wanted to ask a couple of things before I decide — is water usually okay here?"

Then, whichever of these fit:

- "What time does water come, and does it change in summer?"
- "How often does the power go, and does the generator cover the flats?"
- "Is it noisy at night — the road, or a function hall, or construction nearby?"
- "How is it here after dark? Would you be comfortable walking back at ten?"
- "Is parking a problem in the evenings?"
- "Any water-logging on this road during the rains?"

And then the two questions almost nobody asks, both aimed at the watchman:

> "Was the last tenant here happy? Did they leave on good terms with the owner?"

> "Do people usually get their deposit back from this owner without trouble?"

A watchman who has been in a building five years knows which owners settle up and which ones don't. He's seen the arguments in the lobby. He will very often just tell you, because you asked kindly and because he has no stake in the answer.

Tip the conversation, not the man — don't offer money for information, it changes the answer. A genuinely warm two minutes gets you more than a hundred-rupee note does.

## The previous tenant, if you can reach them

Occasionally you can. The owner may offer a reference — a good sign in itself. The watchman may have a number.

If you get through, you only really need one question:

> "Did you get your deposit back, and how long did it take?"

Everything else is a bonus. That single answer tells you how the last week of your tenancy is likely to go, which is the part of renting that goes wrong most often and hurts most when it does.

Follow up with: "Anything about the flat you wish you'd known before moving in?" People are surprisingly generous with a stranger who's about to inherit their problems.

## Questions to ask yourself, honestly

Three, and they're the ones people fudge.

**"Have I done this commute at the time I'd actually be doing it?"** Not on a map app at 2pm on a Sunday. On a Tuesday at 9am, in the direction you'd be travelling. If you're still choosing an area rather than a flat, our notes on the [best areas to live in Chennai](/blog/best-areas-to-live-in-chennai) are written around exactly this trade-off.

**"Can I afford this including the month I move?"** Rent is the small part. Deposit, advance maintenance, movers, a gas connection, curtains, the deposit you haven't got back from your current place yet. If the flat only works assuming everything goes right, it doesn't work.

**"Am I talking myself into this because I'm tired of looking?"** Search fatigue is the most reliable cause of bad rental decisions. Recognising it doesn't make it go away, but it does make you slow down for one more day.

## How to ask without souring things

Tone does most of the work here. A few things that genuinely help:

- **Ask in person, not over text.** You need the pause before the answer, and you can't hear a pause in WhatsApp.
- **Ask as though the answer is normal.** "How long has it been vacant?" delivered casually gets a real answer. Delivered as an accusation gets a defensive one.
- **Bundle the hard ones with easy ones.** Paint colour, then water hours, then parking.
- **Be a good prospect while you're at it.** Mention that you're stable, that you pay on time, that you're not looking to move again in six months. Owners answer honestly when they think you're worth being honest with.
- **Write the answers down afterwards, in your phone.** You will view four flats and merge them in your memory within a week.
- **Then get the important ones in writing.** A verbal "of course I'll return the deposit in fifteen days" is worth exactly what the agreement says it's worth.

None of this makes you difficult. In practice, the renters who ask careful questions are the ones owners *prefer* — because a person who asks about the notice period is a person who plans to honour it.

## Reading the answers

The answer matters less than the shape of it. Here's the pattern that repeats:

| What you ask | What a good answer sounds like | What should worry you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total move-in amount | A single figure, broken down without hesitation | "We'll work it out" — or a number that grows each time you ask |
| What maintenance covers | Named items, and who pays | "Standard maintenance, same as everyone" |
| When the deposit returns | A period and a method, plus what gets adjusted | "Once you vacate we'll settle" |
| Would repainting be deducted | A clear yes or no, and the basis | Changing the subject |
| Water hours | Actual hours, and what changes in summer | "Water is never a problem here" |
| What the last tenant complained about | A real, specific, small complaint | "Nobody has ever complained" |
| Why they left | A concrete life reason | Vagueness, or irritation at the question |
| How long it's been vacant | A number, offered easily | An underestimate you can check with the watchman |
| Lock-in and notice | Both directions, stated plainly | "That's all in the standard agreement" |
| Can we put that in the agreement | "Sure" | "It's not necessary, you can trust me" |

Two rules for reading answers:

**A vague answer to a specific question is itself an answer.** Not proof of bad faith — some owners genuinely don't know their own building's water schedule. But it tells you they're not the person who'll fix things quickly either.

**Cross-check one claim.** Just one. Whatever the owner says about water, ask the watchman about water. If the two match, extend more trust to everything else you were told. If they don't, you've learned the most important thing about this transaction before signing anything — and refusing to put a verbal promise in writing is where both ordinary carelessness and outright [rental scams](/blog/rental-scams-in-india) become visible.

## Where StayOnMap helps, and where it doesn't

Some of these questions shouldn't need asking at all, so we removed them.

Rent, deposit and maintenance are required fields on every listing — it can't go live without them. So the arithmetic on the first money question is largely done before you pick up the phone, and if the figure you hear at the viewing differs from the one on the listing, you have something concrete to ask about.

There's no brokerage, because there's no broker. And when you message about a flat, you're messaging the owner — so the person answering "would repainting be deducted from my deposit" is the person who decides the answer, not someone relaying it.

That's the extent of it. We can't tell you what the water is like at 6am in April, and no listing platform anywhere can. That's still a conversation with a watchman on a Tuesday evening.

## Before you sign

Go back to your notes. Look for three things:

1. **A total number** for what leaves your account before you get the keys, and a receipt for it.
2. **A specific answer** on the deposit — when, how, what gets deducted, is repainting yours.
3. **At least one independent confirmation** from a neighbour or the watchman about the thing you care about most, whether that's water, safety after dark, or noise.

Pair that with a proper walk-through — the [house-hunting checklist](/blog/house-hunting-checklist-india) covers what to physically look at, open, switch on and test, which is the other half of this job.

One last thing. If these questions make an owner irritated rather than merely bored, pay attention. You're seeing exactly how they'll respond in month seven when the motor fails and you call them on a Sunday.

Ask on the stairs. It's cheaper than finding out in April.
